This article is about WTA number 1 rankings since 1975. For the all-time list, see World number 1 ranked female tennis players.
The WTA rankings are the Women's Tennis Association's (WTA) merit-based system for determining the rankings in women's tennis. The top-ranked singles player is the player who, over the previous 52 weeks, has garnered the most ranking points on the WTA Tour. Points are awarded based on how far a player advances in tournaments and the category of those tournaments. The WTA has used a computerized system for determining the rankings since November 3, 1975. Since 1975, 29 women have been ranked No. 1 in singles by the WTA, of which 16 have been year-end No. 1.
Aryna Sabalenka is the current singles world No. 1.

The WTA rankings are the ratings defined by the Women's Tennis Association, introduced in November 1975. The computer that calculates the ranking is nicknamed "Medusa".
Aryna Sabalenka is the current world No. 1 in women's singles.
The WTA rankings are based on a rolling 52-week, cumulative system. A player's ranking is determined by her results at a maximum of 18 tournaments (or 19 if she competed in the WTA Finals) for singles and 12 for doubles. Points are awarded based on how far a player advances in a tournament. The basis for calculating a player's ranking are those tournaments that yield the highest ranking points during the rolling 52-week period. For singles, the period must include:
six WTA 1000 Mandatory combined/virtually combined tournaments
one WTA 1000 Mandatory (WTA-only) tournament
the best of seven results from all WTA 1000 Mandatory, WTA 500, WTA 250, and WTA 125 Tournaments and ITF W15+ events
the WTA Finals as a bonus tournament if the player attended
For doubles, the best 12 tournament results across all tournament levels are used. Unlike singles, there are no specific tournament level requirements and the WTA Finals are not treated as a bonus tournament, instead they are one of the 12 if applicable.
Up until 2016, the WTA also distributed ranking points, for singles players only, who competed at the Summer Olympics. However, this has since been discontinued.
In order to appear on the WTA rankings, players must earn ranking points in at least three tournaments, or a minimum of 10 singles ranking points or 10 doubles ranking points in one or more tournaments.

WTA Singles World Rankings - complete list: Sabalenka hits 100 weeks at the top, Rybakina close second
Discover the top 100 women's singles players in the world right now, as the best tennis players battle for glory on the WTA Tour.
Picture by Matthias Hangst/Getty Images
Who is the best female tennis player in the world?
Based on the WTA singles rankings, Aryna Sabalenka remains the long-undisputed world No.1.
After rising to the top in October 2024, it has now been over 100 weeks at the ranking's summit for the 28-year-old.
The 2026 Laureus World Sportswoman of the Year has won four Grand Slam titles so far, with three singles trophies this season.
Despite Sabalenka’s loss in the fourth round of Wimbledon, she managed to hold off world No.2 Elena Rybakina’s charge for top position after the latter exited one round earlier. The gap between the pair currently stands at 494 points.
After making the Wimbledon quarter-finals for the second time, USA's top-ranked player Jessica Pegula has climbed to the world No.3 spot she last held exactly a year prior. Fellow USA star Coco Gauff sits at world No. 4 heading into the North American hard court swing, ahead of French Open champion Mirra Andreeva.
Czech compatriots Karolína Muchová and Linda Nosková share the sixth and seventh spots respectively, after they shared Centre Court in the Wimbledon women's singles final.
The top 10 is rounded out by six-time major champion Iga Świątek, two-time Grand Slam finalist Amanda Anisimova and Olympic bronze medallist Elina Svitolina.
